newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity seen rising with weather, natgas.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity seen rising with weather, natgas.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were expected to open higher Thursday, particularly the Palo Verde contract, due to expected cooling demand and a rise in natural gas prices, industry sources said.
In early over-the-counter discussion Thursday, May Palo Verde (PV) was assessed at $16.70-17.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) from Wednesday's futures settlement at $16.45 per MWh.
May California Oregon Border (COB) was seen at $12.90-13.10 in early over-the-counter talk from Wednesday's futures settle at $12.99 per MWh.
Forecasts called for much above normal temperatures in the U.S. Southwest over the short term, which traders said was expected to boost cooling demand and give the futures some strength.
Temperatures in the Southwest were expected to average three to 15 degrees Fahrenheit above normal through Sunday, with the greatest departures from normal expected in Nevada, Utah and Colorado.
Southwest temperatures were expected to return to more normal levels early next week with little or no precipitation through Tuesday.
In the Pacific Northwest, temperatures were expected to be four to 10 degrees above normal through early next week under clouds, rain and high mountain snows Saturday and Sunday.

Electricity futures ended higher Wednesday, with traders citing forecasts of above-normal temperatures in the U.S. Southwest, strong natural gas prices, and continued cool weather at high elevations in the Pacific Northwest for the increase.

The weather conditions in higher elevations in the Pacific Northwest were said to have slowed inflows into hydroelectric projects at the same time spill requirements have begun at some dams as an aid to annual fish migration.
NYMEX May Henry Hub natural gas futures opened up about 2.5 cents at $2.03 per million British thermal units on Thursday, with strength said to be coming from higher physical gas prices.
In California, the 1,080 megawatt (MW) San Onofre 3 nuclear power unit remained shut for refueling and maintenance, with an expected restart date near mid-June.
The 1,158 MW WNP-2 nuclear plant in Washington state was also shut for refueling, and was expected to resume power output in early July.
Over 10 coal, fuel and hydroelectric generation units were also said to be out of service in the West for unplanned repair work or spring maintenance.
Also, the 1,087 MW Diablo Canyon nuclear unit 1 in California was expected to begin a refueling outage on April 19 which was seen lasting about two months.
